References / Editorial / 311

Ray Gun Bryan Ferry interview
in Zapf Dingbats

The 1994 Ray Gun spread in which David Carson set a whole Bryan Ferry interview in the symbol font Zapf Dingbats.

Source
Sharan Shetty, “The Rise And Fall Of Grunge Typography”, The Awl (2012), archived copy
Creator
David Carson
Made
1994 (The Awl); issue number not stated by the sources
Style
Grunge typography (partial fit; agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Provocative, chaotic, ironic
Evidence
Inspected a 1100 × 697 photograph of the opened spread, posted on the Process & Skills student blog (2013), in a scratchpad copy; The Awl’s own copy is 640 px wide. The owner of the photographed copy and the issue number are not stated. Not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The Awl says Carson disliked a Ray Gun article on Bryan Ferry and set the entire spread in Zapf Dingbats, in a 1994 issue. The Awl.

Wikipedia cites the Ferry interview as the example of Ray Gun’s not always readable “grunge typography”. Wikipedia).

Observed

  • The right-hand page and most of the left are justified columns made entirely of Zapf Dingbats symbols: stars, circles, triangles, crosses, and arrows.
  • A grey rectangle sits behind part of the dingbat text and crosses the gutter.
  • The headline “bryan ferry” is a lowercase serif, partly covered by a large maroon four-lobed dingbat and a yellow-green photograph of Ferry in an armchair.
  • A large olive asterisk-like dingbat and a row of grey stars and flowers act as display ornaments.
  • The photo credit under the picture is the only readable text.

Why it belongs

The spread is grunge as a gesture rather than as a texture: it uses a clean, standard font to make text unreadable. It belongs in the collection for its intent and for how often it is cited, not for its surfaces.

Borrow

Use a symbol font as a grey texture that has the rhythm of text, in a decorative area only.

Enlarge single dingbats to poster size and let them cover a headline.
